title: Seeing and being seen
text:
On the chart you only see the fleets your lookouts or radar can reach. A fleet that slips out of sight leaves a grey mark where it was last reported; steer for the mark, not for where you hope she is.

How far you see depends on your captain's watch, the weather and the hour. Night, fog and storms cut it sharply. The same rules bind every other fleet: nobody has a sighting distance you lack.

**Running dark.** You can order the squadron to show no lights and keep the wireless silent. You are found from less far off, but your own radar is off too.

**In battle** an enemy ship that is not seen is not drawn. Smoke hides whatever lies behind it. A ship that fires or burns at night shows herself at about twice the usual distance. Press **R** to show the rings: how far your lookouts, radar and sonar reach.

title: Radar, sonar and silence
text:
Radar and sonar find the enemy, and they also announce you. A radar set that is switched on can be heard by any ship with a set of her own from several times further than it can see. A sonar ping is heard by every hydrophone in range.

**Radar (Y).** Sees through night and fog. A rotating set paints a contact once each turn of the aerial, so a ship held by radar alone fades and returns on the plot. Switch it off to stay hidden.

**Sonar (U).** A dived submarine is found by sound alone: guns cannot touch her. Listening is silent, and hears a fast boat from further than a slow one. Pinging finds a quiet boat, and tells her exactly where you are.

**Jamming and chaff.** With electronic countermeasures researched, a ship can jam enemy radar (and is heard doing it), and carries chaff that may draw off a missile in its last seconds.

Right-click one of your ships in battle for her own switches.

title: Gunnery
text:
A ship does not hit with her first salvo. She works out a solution on her target, fires, watches the fall of shot and corrects. Each spotted salvo lands closer. Change target and she starts again.

What helps: radar fire control, a trained crew, a floatplane or drone over the target (**F** on a ship that carries one), a steady course, and daylight.

What hurts: a rough sea, a listing ship, a hit on the director, hard turns by you or the target, and firing at something you cannot see.

**Shells (V).** Armour-piercing defeats armour it can beat and bursts inside; it passes clean through light ships. High explosive wrecks light ships and upper works and starts fires. Incendiary sets fires and little else. Left on automatic, the gunnery officer chooses by target.

**Hold E** to ride the heaviest shell or missile you last fired, and watch it land.

title: Armour and where shells land
text:
A ship is armoured in four places: her belt along the side, her deck, her turrets, and the citadel that holds magazines and machinery. Her bow and stern are soft.

At short range shells arrive flat and meet the belt. At long range they plunge and meet the deck, which is thinner. So a ship with a thick belt and a thin deck wants to fight close, and one with a good deck can stand off.

A shell that cannot beat the armour in front of it does little. One that beats it by a wide margin may pass straight through a small ship without bursting.

Missiles are different. A belt keeps out part of a sea-skimmer's blast, but what stands above the armour does not survive: light guns, directors, radar, and fires every time. A heavy missile is stopped by very little.

Armour is worn down by hits, and can be added or landed in a yard refit, at a cost in weight.

title: Damage control
text:
A hit does more than lower a number. Where it lands decides what it reaches: a magazine under a turret, machinery amidships, steering right aft, the director in the bridge, crew spaces forward.

**Fires** burn until they are put out, and spread damage while they burn. **Flooding** gives the ship a list: she turns badly, loses speed, and her guns shoot worse.

**Priorities (B).** Tell damage control what to fight first: fire, flooding or machinery. The other two go slower.

**Flood the magazine (N).** A fire in a magazine will destroy the ship if it reaches the charges. Flooding it saves her and costs you the turret above.

**Counter-flood (J).** Let the sea into the high side to bring her upright at once. She fights level again, but the water stays aboard and slows her for the rest of the action.

A ship that sinks slowly may be raised afterwards if you hold the field.

title: Torpedoes, missiles and your own side
text:
Every weapon hurts whatever it strikes, friend or enemy.

**Torpedoes (T)** run straight and hit the first hull in their path. Their reach is short, well inside a destroyer's guns, so the attacker must close. Homing torpedoes run deaf until near the aim point, then go for the nearest ship they hear, whatever her flag. Your captains will not fire with a friend in the track; if you try, you are warned and must press again.

**Depth charges (Z)** are dropped in a pattern over where a submarine will be. They also hurt a slow ship above them, your own included.

**Missiles (Q)** fly low and unseen until close, or high and visible. Close-in guns and anti-aircraft missiles shoot some down. Wartime light guns stop very few.

**Shells** are tested against every ship where they land. Captains check fire when a friend lies near the point of aim. Your flagship's hand-laid guns are your own affair.

title: Orders in battle
text:
Keys **1 to 8** give the squadron its order: engage freely, form on the flag, line ahead, line abreast, screen, withdraw, hold fire, make smoke.

Click a ship of yours to give her an order of her own; Shift+click picks several. **Tab** shifts your flag to the next ship.

**Your orders stand (O).** A ship left under your own orders keeps the course, speed and waypoints you gave her when you move to another ship. Her captain does not take her out of action on his own. Switch it off and he fights her as he sees fit.

**Division leads.** Ships can form on any ship, not only the flagship. Right-click the lead and choose "form on her".

**Stations.** "Keep present stations" holds the squadron in the shape it lies in now; "standard stations" puts it back.

**Marks beside a ship's name** show a state you set: a pennant for your own orders, chevrons for a ship formed on another lead, a diamond for a station you gave her. Her menu then offers "back to normal" first.

Captains have tempers. A bold one closes and fights on when hurt; a cautious one keeps the range open and pulls out early.

title: Refits by weight
text:
A hull can carry only so much. Every gun, launcher and system has a weight, and weight carried high counts for more.

The yard's ledger shows what a new fit does: tons over or under the ship as built, and how top-heavy she is. A little over costs speed. More costs helm, and her salvos scatter. Far over, the yard refuses. Landing weight gives a little speed back.

A mount takes a gun about the size of the one it was built for. A side mount has less room than one on the centreline.

A refit is done at once, but it costs the crew's readiness. An old ship can be reconstructed in a yard to wear like a younger one, and a ship raised from the bottom carries defects until she is rebuilt.

Ships of the missile age carry the missiles and guns they were designed with. Older hulls need the research before they can take them.

title: Supply, readiness and wear
text:
There is no fixed limit on ships. There is a limit on what you can supply. Every ship weighs on the supply train by her size; oilers, store ships and repair ships add to what you can carry, as do a navy you serve and harbours you hold. Over the limit, crews tire and cannot be kept fresh.

**Readiness** falls at sea, faster at speed and in bad weather, and recovers in port or hove to. Tired ships reload, steam and fight fires slower.

**Fuel** burns by the day, and steeply faster at high speed. Out of fuel you drift: call a tow or a passing oiler by wireless.

**Wear** grows with time under way, faster in an old ship, and costs speed until an overhaul in port.

**Laying up.** A ship you do not need can be laid up in a harbour for a small daily fee. She costs no crew or supply, and is seized if that harbour's flag goes to war with you.

Ten ships at most fight in one action; the rest stand off.

title: Your own flag
text:
A captain can raise a flag of his own. From then you may hold harbours, and the powers must decide what to make of you.

**Taking a harbour** means landing troops against its garrison; troopships carry them. A held harbour pays dues, runs a yard and can be given works that feed its trade.

**Holding it** means guard squadrons and convoys of your own, and relief forces coming to take it back.

**The Chancery** is where you ask the powers for recognition, treaties and peace. A treaty stops every hostile act of that power.

**Coalitions and wars.** You can join a coalition, leave it, or declare war yourself. You can post notices and hire patrols.

Choose a capital, and a device for your ensign, which your ships then fly in battle.

title: Weather and night
text:
Weather comes from where you are and the time of year. It is the same for everyone.

**Night** cuts sighting hard. A moon helps. Star shell (**G**) lights a patch of sea for a while: ships under it are seen as by day.

**Fog** blinds lookouts, not radar.

**Storms** slow small ships, spoil gunnery, burn more fuel, stop aircraft flying and tire crews faster.

**Ice** closes the far north for much of the year and costs fuel to push through.

Aircraft do not fly in a storm or fog. Only jets fly by night; drones fly by night and in fog.

title: Carriers and aircraft
text:
Aircraft leave and return to a carrier one at a time, so a strike takes time to fly off and time to land. A holed flight deck stops all flying until it is patched.

**Strike (F).** Propeller aircraft carry torpedoes and bombs. Jets carry stand-off missiles and bombs, and let the missiles go from well outside gun range.

Anti-aircraft guns and fighters thin a strike on its way in. Aircraft whose carrier is lost make for another deck of their side.

**Floatplanes and drones.** Cruisers and battleships with catapults carry floatplanes; modern warships carry a drone. Over the target they call the fall of shot and see over smoke.

**From the land.** An enemy airfield that has found you may send a raid, by day in flying weather.
